notes: Daniel mixes court-narrative (chs 1-6) with apocalyptic vision-report (chs 7-12); KJV renders portions in Hebrew (1:1-2:4a; 8:1-12:13) and Aramaic (2:4b-7:28) but this does not affect character indexing. Scribe tiers are object/motif names tied to each major figure's or law's defining scene, following the Genesis-established pattern. Two distinct heavenly messengers appear in the book's back half — Gabriel (explicitly named, chs 8-9) and the unnamed 'man clothed in linen' (ch 10, 12) — and are deliberately NOT identified with each other here, since the text itself never equates them. The book has no extended named genealogies (unlike Genesis/Chronicles/Ezra-Nehemiah), so genealogyLists is empty. Corrected from a prior draft that miscounted Daniel's 'greatly beloved' citations as two when three verses (9:23, 10:11, 10:19) use the phrase.

scribeTiers.scribeName: The Dream-Image of Gold and Clay

characters.name: Daniel

genealogy.note: Not named in the book. Daniel is identified as one of 'the children of Judah' among the royal/noble youths taken captive to Babylon (1:3-6), and later called 'that Daniel, which art of the children of the captivity of Judah' by Belshazzar (5:13).

funFacts: Renamed Belteshazzar by the prince of the eunuchs (1:7) — not to be confused with King Belshazzar of chapter 5, a different person with a similar-looking name.
Purposed in his heart not to defile himself with the king's food, and proposed a ten-day vegetable-and-water trial instead (1:8-14).
Interpreted Nebuchadnezzar's dream of the great multi-metal image after it was revealed to him in a night vision (2:19-45).
Made ruler over the whole province of Babylon and chief of the governors over all its wise men (2:48).
Continued praying toward Jerusalem three times a day, kneeling with his windows open, even after Darius's thirty-day prayer ban (6:10).
Spent a night in the lions' den and came out with 'no manner of hurt' found upon him, 'because he believed in his God' (6:23).
Called 'greatly beloved' three times by heavenly messengers across two visions (9:23, 10:11, 10:19).
Mourned and fasted three full weeks, eating no pleasant bread, flesh, or wine, before receiving his final vision (10:2-3).
The book closes with him told to 'go thy way till the end be' and that he will 'stand in thy lot at the end of the days' (12:13).

verses.note: Purposed in his heart not to defile himself with the king's meat and wine.
Found ten times better than all the magicians and astrologers in the realm.
The secret of Nebuchadnezzar's dream revealed to Daniel in a night vision.
Made ruler over the whole province of Babylon and chief governor over all the wise men.
Prayed toward Jerusalem three times a day with his windows open, despite the new decree.
Testifies God sent his angel and shut the lions' mouths.
Called 'greatly beloved' by the messenger sent at the beginning of his supplication.
Called 'a man greatly beloved' by the being who appears to him by the great river Hiddekel.
Called 'O man greatly beloved' again in the same vision, told 'fear not... be strong.'
Told to 'go thy way till the end be,' and that he will 'stand in thy lot at the end of the days.'

characters.perkNote: Represents unwavering devotion under pressure — named 'greatly beloved' three separate times by heavenly messengers (9:23, 10:11, 10:19).

characters.name: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego

genealogy.note: Parents not named. Identified together with Daniel as being 'of the children of Judah' (1:6), given their Babylonian names by the prince of the eunuchs in place of their Hebrew names Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah (1:7). They always act as a single collective unit in the narrative, never distinguished individually.

funFacts: Original Hebrew names were Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, changed by the prince of the eunuchs to Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego (1:7).
Joined Daniel in the ten-day pulse-and-water trial and were likewise found 'ten times better' than all the magicians and astrologers (1:15-20).
Set over the affairs of the province of Babylon at Daniel's request, while Daniel himself remained 'in the gate of the king' (2:49).
Refused outright to serve Nebuchadnezzar's gods or worship the golden image, telling the king to his face they would not, even if God chose not to deliver them (3:16-18).
Thrown into a furnace heated seven times hotter than usual, yet walked unbound and unharmed; Nebuchadnezzar himself remarked on seeing a fourth figure in the fire (3:19-25).
Came out with not even the smell of fire on their clothes, and were promoted in the province of Babylon afterward (3:27-30).

verses.note: Given the names Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in place of Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah.
Set by Daniel's request over the affairs of the province of Babylon.
Accused before Nebuchadnezzar of refusing to serve his gods or worship the golden image.
Declare God is able to deliver them from the furnace, but that they will not worship the image even if He does not.
Nebuchadnezzar sees a fourth figure walking with them in the fire, 'like the Son of God' (the king's own description).
Come out of the furnace with no harm, not even the smell of fire upon them.

characters.perkNote: Represents strength in refusing to bend together — 'we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image' (3:18).

characters.name: The King's Portion (Ten-Day Test)
characters.purpose: Tests whether faithfulness to God's dietary conviction can be maintained even under royal pressure to defile oneself with the king's rich food and wine; demonstrates that trust in God's provision outperforms the king's own fare (1:15-16, 1:20). (Attribution: Proposed by Daniel to Melzar the steward (Daniel 1:8-13))
funFacts: The whole test was Daniel's own proposal, not a command imposed on him (1:8, 1:11-13).
Ran for exactly ten days by Daniel's own proposed terms (1:12-14).
The result: the four youths looked 'fairer and fatter in flesh' than those who ate the king's meat (1:15).

verses.note: Daniel purposes not to defile himself with the king's meat and wine.
Proposes a ten-day trial of pulse and water to Melzar.
At the end of ten days they appear fairer and fatter than the others.
Found ten times better than all the magicians and astrologers.

characters.perkNote: Represents provision outperforming excess — pulse and water leaving the four 'fairer and fatter' than the king's own meat (1:15).

characters.name: Nebuchadnezzar
characters.scribeTier: The Dream-Image of Gold and Clay

children: Belshazzar (per the text's own repeated use of 'father,' 5:2, 5:11, 5:13, 5:18)
genealogy.note: Parents not named in Daniel. The book repeatedly calls him Belshazzar's 'father' (5:2, 5:11, 5:13, 5:18), and the queen calls him 'thy father' (5:11) — the text's own term for the relationship. KJV Daniel consistently spells the name 'Nebuchadnezzar,' distinct from the 'Nebuchadrezzar' spelling used for the same king in Jeremiah and Ezekiel — a deliberate KJV spelling difference, not normalized here.

funFacts: Besieged Jerusalem and carried off vessels from the house of God to the treasure house of his own god (1:1-2).
Demanded his wise men state both his dream and its interpretation without being told the dream, threatening to have them 'cut in pieces' if they failed (2:5-9).
Fell on his face and worshipped before Daniel after the dream was correctly told and interpreted, acknowledging Daniel's God as 'a God of gods' (2:46-47).
Later had a second dream, of a great tree cut down, which Daniel interpreted as a personal warning to him (4:19-27).

Judged within the year for boasting of 'great Babylon, that I have built' — driven from men to eat grass like oxen for 'seven times,' with hair like eagles' feathers and nails like birds' claws (4:28-33).
Reason and honor were restored to him at the end of the appointed time, and he closes his own words in the book praising 'the King of heaven,' who is able to abase the proud (4:34-37).

verses.note: Besieges Jerusalem and carries off vessels of the house of God to Babylon.
Demands the wise men tell both his dream and its interpretation, on pain of being cut in pieces.
Falls on his face before Daniel and acknowledges Daniel's God as 'a God of gods.'
Sets up the golden image in the plain of Dura.
Boasts of 'great Babylon, that I have built... by the might of my power.'
Driven from men, eats grass like oxen, hair grown like eagles' feathers, nails like birds' claws.
Reason restored; praises and honors the King of heaven, who is able to abase the proud.

characters.perkNote: Represents the king's swing from towering pride ('great Babylon, that I have built,' 4:30) to complete humbling (4:33) and eventual restoration (4:36-37).

characters.name: The Golden Image of Dura
characters.purpose: Demands universal worship of a ninety-foot golden image at the sound of royal music, on pain of death by fire; becomes the test of the three Hebrews' exclusive loyalty to God (3:12, 3:16-18). (Attribution: Decreed by King Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 3:1-6))
funFacts: The image measured 'threescore cubits' high and 'six cubits' wide, set up in the plain of Dura in the province of Babylon (3:1).
All peoples, nations, and languages were commanded to fall down and worship it at the sound of a specific list of instruments (3:4-7).
The furnace was ordered heated seven times hotter than usual specifically because of Nebuchadnezzar's fury at the three Hebrews' refusal (3:19).
Nebuchadnezzar himself — not the three men — is the one who describes seeing a fourth figure in the fire, saying its form is 'like the Son of God' (3:25).

verses.note: Nebuchadnezzar sets up the image, threescore cubits high, in the plain of Dura.
All peoples commanded to fall down and worship at the sound of the music, or be cast into a burning fiery furnace.
Furnace heated seven times hotter than usual.
Nebuchadnezzar blesses their God and decrees against any who speak against Him.

characters.perkNote: Represents the cost of public defiance turned into public vindication — the furnace that could not even singe them (3:27).

characters.name: Belshazzar

genealogy.father: Nebuchadnezzar (per the text's own repeated term 'father,' 5:2, 5:11, 5:13, 5:18)
genealogy.note: Caution: 'Belshazzar' (the king of chapter 5) is easily confused with 'Belteshazzar,' the separate Babylonian name given to Daniel (1:7) — two distinct people with similar-looking names. The unnamed 'queen' who advises him in 5:10-12 is not identified further by the text.

funFacts: Made a great feast for a thousand of his lords and commanded that the gold and silver vessels his father Nebuchadnezzar had taken from the Jerusalem temple be brought in so the guests could drink from them (5:1-3).
Praised the gods of gold, silver, brass, iron, wood, and stone at the same feast (5:4).
His countenance changed and his knees 'smote one against another' at the sight of the hand writing on the wall (5:6).
Offered to make Daniel 'third ruler in the kingdom' for reading and interpreting the writing — Daniel read it despite refusing the offered rewards (5:16-17, 29).
Slain that same night, and the kingdom passed to Darius the Mede (5:30-31).
The text repeatedly calls Nebuchadnezzar his 'father' (5:2, 11, 13, 18) — the book's own term for the relationship.

verses.note: Makes a great feast and commands the temple vessels his father Nebuchadnezzar had taken be brought in for drinking.
Sees fingers of a man's hand writing on the wall; his countenance changes and his knees smite together.
Daniel reads and interprets MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN.
Makes Daniel the third ruler in the kingdom despite the judgment just pronounced.
Slain that same night; Babylon falls.

characters.perkNote: Represents misuse of what wasn't his to use — drinking from the temple vessels his father had taken (5:2-4), judged that same night (5:30).

characters.name: The Handwriting on the Wall
characters.purpose: Pronounces immediate divine judgment on Belshazzar for profaning the temple vessels and exalting himself against the God of heaven (5:22-23); announces the fall of Babylon that very night. (Attribution: Written by fingers of a man's hand sent out from an unnamed, undescribed source (Daniel 5:5), interpreted by Daniel (5:25-28))
funFacts: The hand that writes is described only as 'fingers of a man's hand,' with no figure attached to it ever named or described further (5:5).
The words themselves are MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN (5:25).
None of Belshazzar's own wise men could read or interpret it, though the queen recalled that Daniel had done similar things for Nebuchadnezzar (5:8, 5:10-12).
Daniel's interpretation ties the words to counting, weighing, and dividing the kingdom (5:26-28), fulfilled that same night (5:30).

verses.note: Fingers of a man's hand appear and write over against the candlestick.
The writing: MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN.
Daniel's interpretation of each word.
Belshazzar slain that night.

characters.perkNote: Represents an instant, unappealable verdict — 'weighed in the balances, and art found wanting' (5:27).

characters.name: Darius the Mede

genealogy.father: Ahasuerus, 'of the seed of the Medes' (9:1) — a different Ahasuerus from the Persian king Ahasuerus/Xerxes of the book of Esther, and from the Ahasuerus named in Ezra 4:6; the three should not be conflated.
genealogy.note: Distinct from 'Darius' the Persian king (Darius I) named later in Ezra, Haggai, and Zechariah — Daniel's own text specifically titles this king 'Darius the Mede' (5:31, 6:1, 9:1, 11:1).

ageEvents.event: Took the kingdom of Babylon, being 'about threescore and two years old'

funFacts: Took the kingdom at about sixty-two years old (5:31).
Set 120 princes over the kingdom and three presidents, including Daniel, whom he considered setting over the whole realm (6:1-3).
The presidents and princes, unable to find any fault in Daniel, used his faithfulness to God against him via a decree they tricked Darius into signing (6:4-9).
Labored until sundown trying to find a way to deliver Daniel, but could not overturn a law of the Medes and Persians once sealed (6:14-15).
Passed the night fasting, with no instruments of music brought before him, and could not sleep (6:18).
Went to the den at dawn and cried out 'with a lamentable voice' to ask if Daniel's God had been able to deliver him (6:19-20).
Had Daniel's accusers, along with their children and wives, cast into the den in his place (6:24).
Identified as 'the son of Ahasuerus, of the seed of the Medes' (9:1) — distinct from the Ahasuerus of the book of Esther, a later Persian king.

verses.note: Takes the kingdom at about sixty-two years old.
Considers setting Daniel over the whole realm for his excellent spirit.
Labors till sundown to try to deliver Daniel from the decree.
Casts Daniel into the lions' den, telling him 'thy God... will deliver thee.'
Rises early and goes to the den 'with a lamentable voice.'
Decrees that all in his dominion tremble and fear before the God of Daniel.
Identified as 'Darius the son of Ahasuerus, of the seed of the Medes.'

characters.perkNote: Represents a ruler who fights for his subordinate within the limits of his own law — labors till sundown to save Daniel (6:14), then reverses course entirely once vindicated (6:24-27).

characters.name: Gabriel

genealogy.note: An angelic messenger, not a human genealogical figure. Explicitly named 'the man Gabriel' (8:16; 9:21) and described as having 'the appearance of a man' (8:15). Not to be conflated with the unnamed 'man clothed in linen' of Daniel 10:5-6 and 12:6-7 — the text itself never states these are the same figure.

funFacts: Explicitly named 'the man Gabriel' on both of his appearances to Daniel (8:16; 9:21).
His appearance in chapter 8 was overwhelming enough that Daniel fell on his face and 'fainted, and was sick certain days' (8:17-18, 27).
Sent specifically to interpret the vision of the ram and the he-goat (8:16-26).
Returns in chapter 9 'caused to fly swiftly' and touches Daniel about the time of the evening oblation, then delivers the seventy weeks prophecy (9:21-27).
Not to be confused with the separate, unnamed 'man clothed in linen' of chapters 10 and 12 — the text never states these are the same figure.

verses.note: Named directly: a man's voice calls, 'Gabriel, make this man to understand the vision.'
Daniel falls on his face and faints at his approach; Gabriel touches him and sets him upright.
Identified again as 'the man Gabriel,' caused to fly swiftly and touch Daniel at the time of evening oblation.
Comes to give Daniel 'skill and understanding,' calling him 'greatly beloved.'
Delivers the seventy weeks prophecy.

characters.perkNote: Represents interpretive insight delivered directly — sent specifically 'to give thee skill and understanding' (9:22).

characters.name: The Seventy Weeks Prophecy
characters.purpose: Lays out a specific prophetic timetable — seventy weeks 'determined upon thy people and upon thy holy city' — to finish transgression, make an end of sins, bring in everlasting righteousness, and anoint the most holy (9:24-27). (Attribution: Delivered to Daniel by the angel Gabriel while Daniel prayed (Daniel 9:20-23))
funFacts: Given as a direct answer to Daniel's prayer of confession on behalf of his people, offered while he was still speaking (9:20-23).
Specifies a total of seventy weeks 'determined upon thy people and upon thy holy city' (9:24).
Breaks the seventy weeks into sub-periods — seven weeks, sixty-two weeks, and a final week — each tied to specific events (9:25-27).

verses.note: Given by Gabriel while Daniel is still speaking in prayer.
Seventy weeks determined to finish transgression, make an end of sins, and anoint the most holy.
Lays out the sequence: rebuilding Jerusalem, the coming of Messiah the Prince, and events after.

characters.perkNote: Represents a single fixed prophetic timetable laid out in full at once (9:24-27).

characters.name: Ashpenaz

genealogy.note: Genealogy not stated; identified only by his office, 'master of his eunuchs' (1:3).

funFacts: Titled 'master of his eunuchs' and given the task of selecting royal and noble Israelite youths for the king's service (1:3-4).
Personally renamed Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah with their Babylonian names (1:7).
God specifically gave Daniel 'favour and tender love' in his sight (1:9).
Worried aloud that if the youths looked worse than their peers, the king would have his own head for it (1:10).

verses.note: Commanded by Nebuchadnezzar to bring in certain of the children of Israel of the royal seed and the princes.
Gives Daniel and his three companions their Babylonian names.
God brings Daniel into favour and tender love with him.
Fears the king will see the youths' faces worse-favoured and have him beheaded.

characters.perkNote: Brings Daniel into 'favour and tender love' at court (1:9), easing his rise before he's even proven himself.

characters.name: Melzar

genealogy.note: Genealogy not stated. KJV renders 'the Melzar' with the definite article both times he appears (1:11, 1:16), which may indicate a title/office rather than a proper personal name — flagged here rather than treated as certain.

funFacts: KJV writes 'the Melzar' with a definite article both times he appears (1:11, 1:16), reading more like a title/office than a personal name.
Agreed to Daniel's proposed ten-day test after Ashpenaz's own reluctance (1:11-14).
Continued taking away the royal diet and giving pulse instead once the trial proved successful (1:16).

verses.note: Set by Ashpenaz over Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah.
Consents to Daniel's proposal and proves them ten days.
Takes away their portion of the king's meat and gives them pulse.

characters.perkNote: Administers the cheaper pulse-and-water diet in place of the king's rich provisions (1:14-16).

characters.name: Arioch

genealogy.note: Genealogy not stated; identified only by his office, 'captain of the king's guard' (2:14).

funFacts: Titled 'captain of the king's guard,' sent out with orders to execute all of Babylon's wise men after they failed to tell Nebuchadnezzar his dream (2:14-15).
Daniel appeals directly to him, 'with counsel and wisdom,' to buy time from the king (2:14-16).
Brings Daniel before the king 'in haste,' presenting himself as the one who found the answer ('I have found a man...'), even though the discovery was Daniel's alone (2:25).

verses.note: Captain of the king's guard, gone forth to slay the wise men of Babylon.
Daniel asks him for time before the king to show the interpretation.
Brings Daniel in hastily before the king, claiming to have found a man of the captives of Judah.

characters.perkNote: Delivers Daniel to the king's attention at a critical moment, taking him from unknown captive to the king's presence in one stroke (2:25).

characters.name: Michael the Archangel

genealogy.note: An angelic figure, not a human genealogical one. Called 'one of the chief princes' (10:13) and 'the great prince which standeth for the children of thy people' (12:1).

funFacts: Called 'one of the chief princes' who comes to help the speaker of chapter 10 against 'the prince of the kingdom of Persia' (10:13).
Referred to as 'your prince,' i.e., Israel's own angelic prince (10:21).
In the final chapter, he is the 'great prince which standeth for the children of thy people,' whose standing up marks 'a time of trouble, such as never was' (12:1).

verses.note: Called 'one of the chief princes,' comes to help the speaker against the prince of the kingdom of Persia.
Called 'Michael your prince.'
Called 'the great prince which standeth for the children of thy people,' who shall 'stand up' at the time of the end.

characters.perkNote: Arrives to help tip a contested angelic conflict, described as coming to help against 'the prince of the kingdom of Persia' (10:13).
